name: Veena
definition: Veena is a composite portrait of a woman supervisor in one of the coffee-curing warehouses that ring Chikkamagaluru town, drawn from the experience of Vokkaliga families in Kadur taluk who straddle the border between the coffee belt and the drier plains. She represents households where one foot is in plantation commerce and the other in dryland farming, where daughters have pushed into salaried roles their mothers never held, and where the cost and promise of English-medium schooling dominate family conversation.

topics.label: Daily Life and Work
topics.profile: Veena works six days a week in a coffee-curing and grading unit on the Kadur-Chikkamagaluru road, supervising a floor of twenty women who hand-sort Arabica beans by grade before bagging for export. She arrives by seven-thirty, checks moisture meters, assigns the day's lot to sorters, and stands most of the shift monitoring quality and speed. The unit pays her eleven thousand rupees a month, more than the sorters earn but less than the men who run the roasting drums. Her husband farms five acres of coconut and finger millet near Kadur town; the land gives them security but little cash, so her salary covers school fees, the cylinder, clothes and the instalment on the washing machine. Harvests from October to February mean long days and weekend overtime as beans pour in from Mudigere and Koppa estates; March to September the work slows and she worries each year whether the manager will cut shifts. She keeps her mobile close for price updates and family calls, eats a packed lunch of ragi mudde at noon, and reaches home by six to begin the second shift of cooking and homework supervision.

topics.label: Family and Household
topics.profile: Veena lives in a rented two-room house on Kadur's outskirts with her husband Prakasha, her mother-in-law, and her two sons aged twelve and nine. Prakasha's father died five years ago; the farm passed to Prakasha, the only son, and his mother moved in soon after. Veena's own parents live fifteen kilometres away in a village near Birur; her younger brother runs their father's areca smallholding and her sister married into Hassan. Veena was married at twenty-one after completing her PUC; Prakasha had finished a BA and was farming the family land. Her mother-in-law cooks breakfast and watches the house during the day but expects Veena to cook dinner, manage the boys' homework, and handle all washing and cleaning on Sundays. Veena sends money to her parents when the coffee unit pays a Diwali bonus. She hopes her sons will study past what she managed and find salaried work in a town or city; she tells them the farm is security, not a career, and that English is the ladder her generation never climbed.

topics.label: Education and Schooling
topics.profile: Veena completed her SSLC in a Kannada-medium government high school in her home village and her PUC in a Kadur college, travelling by bus. Her parents wanted her to study further but worried about the cost and the marriage market, so she stopped after second PUC and worked in a tailor's shop until her wedding. Her two sons study in an English-medium CBSE school in Kadur town; the older boy is in seventh standard, the younger in fourth. Fees, uniforms, books and van transport together cost nearly thirty thousand rupees a year, more than half Veena's annual salary. The school has smart classes and computer labs, things Veena never saw, and demands project files and English conversation she cannot help with. She hires a tutor for mathematics twice a week. The boys bring home circulars about Bangalore coaching centres for engineering entrance exams; Veena and Prakasha argue over whether they can afford that path or whether the boys should aim for a BCom and a bank job. Veena insists they will not stop at PUC as she did; the coffee unit and the farm have taught her that only salaried, English-speaking work offers her sons a future Kadur can no longer promise.

topics.label: Health and Wellbeing
topics.profile: Veena's mother-in-law has diabetes and high blood pressure; they spend fifteen hundred rupees a month on her tablets from a private clinic in Kadur, and every few months take her to Chikkamagaluru town for tests. Veena herself has chronic lower-back pain from standing all day on the curing-unit floor; a government hospital doctor gave her ibuprofen and told her to sit more, which her work does not allow. She has borne two children, both deliveries in Kadur's government hospital, both without complication. She worries about her sons' eyesight; the older boy squints at the blackboard and needs glasses they have not yet bought. The family drinks filtered water at home but the boys drink tap water at school. Kadur has a government hospital and several private clinics; for anything serious they would go to Chikkamagaluru or Shivamogga. Veena knows women in the curing unit who have had hysterectomies in their forties; she wonders if standing work and lifting loads cause it. She has heard of Kyasanur Forest Disease in the forest-fringe villages of Koppa but has never seen a case in Kadur. Her mother-in-law's medicines, her own pain, and the boys' health absorb money and worry every month.

topics.label: Community and Belief
topics.profile: Veena's family are Vokkaligas, the dominant farming community in Kadur and across much of Hassan and southern Chikkamagaluru. Her mother-in-law insists on Vokkaliga marriage alliances and watches caste in every social dealing; Veena is less strict but still considers caste when choosing her sons' friends' families. The household worships at a Hanuman temple near Kadur town and celebrates Ugadi, Deepavali and Sankranti with particular care. Veena fasts on Tuesdays for her sons' welfare. Her mother tongue is Kannada; she speaks a plains Kannada closer to Mysuru speech than to the Havyaka or Malnad Kannada of the coffee-belt workers she supervises, some of whom come from Mudigere or Koppa. At work she moves between Kannada with the sorters and broken English and Kannada with the manager and the exporters who visit. She is part of a women's self-help group linked to SKDRDP that meets monthly in Kadur; the group has helped her take a small loan for her sons' school fees. She has friends among the sorters but keeps a supervisor's distance; most are from poorer families or different castes, and mixing too freely would trouble her mother-in-law.

topics.label: Civic Life and Government
topics.profile: The money comes into her bank account each month now and pays for groceries and the boys' school costs her salary cannot cover. She has a ration card that gives her cheap rice and other subsidies. Her husband tried unsuccessfully to get a Raitha Samparka Kendra soil-health card for the farm; the process stalled and he gave up. Veena's self-help group has brought her closer to the anganwadi worker and the gram panchayat than she was before; she now knows which officials to ask when the streetlight outside her house stays broken for weeks. She has never attended a gram sabha herself but her husband goes. She reads Kannada newspapers when she has time and follows news of coffee prices and water disputes. The Kasturirangan environmental report worries her husband and the coffee-estate owners she hears at work; they say it will freeze land and kill livelihoods, and she believes them because she sees how tightly the curing unit's fortunes are tied to the estates. She trusts teachers and doctors more than she trusts politicians or officials.

topics.label: Worldview and Concerns
topics.profile: Veena is proud that she holds a supervisor's job in a man's world of coffee commerce, proud that her sons study in English medium, and proud that her salary gives the household a cushion her mother's generation never had. She worries constantly about money: school fees, her mother-in-law's medicines, the farm's uncertain yields, and what will happen if the coffee unit cuts her shifts in a lean year. She worries that her sons will not keep up with Bangalore children in the race for engineering seats, that the tutor is not enough, that the CBSE school is a gamble they cannot afford to lose. She blames the government for not controlling the price of onions and tomatoes, for letting private schools charge what they like, and for years of empty promises about farm loan waivers that never reach small holders like her husband. She blames herself for stopping at PUC and for not learning English well enough to help her children. She is angry that her back hurts every night and that no doctor takes it seriously, angry that women do the same sorting work as men but earn two thousand rupees less. She wants her sons to leave Kadur for salaried work in a city, and she wants them to remember where they came from and to send money home when the farm needs it.
